title: Keeping It Cool
caption: The McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope, Kitt Peak National Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The decommissioned McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope sits at the center of this photograph from NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). It saw first light in 1962, kept working for 55 years and was retired in 2017. For much of that time it was the largest solar telescope on Earth.

Solar astronomy turns the usual problem around. Most telescopes struggle to collect enough light from faint, distant targets. The Sun is close by astronomical standards and by far the brightest object in the Solar System, so light is plentiful. What comes with it is heat. Sunlight warms the air inside a solar telescope's tunnel, and that warm air distorts the data.

The designers fought the heat with special paint, pipes carrying a cooling liquid, and the natural chill of the ground below. Together these kept the bottom of the 61-meter (200-foot) optical path about 6 °C (11 °F) cooler than the outside air.

explore: Although it no longer observes the Sun, the building has a new purpose. When the photograph was released, NOIRLab was converting it into an outreach facility, NOIRLab's Windows on the Universe Center for Astronomy Outreach. The credit names the photographer as B. Tafreshi.
